fullName: Atomic, high-resolution coherent imaging of atomistic structures at 34-ID-F

status2026.detail: The APS commissioning chart dated 5 October 2026 places '34-ID-F: ATOMIC XSD' at stage 5, 'Scientific Commissioning and Early Experiments'. General-user restart is stage 6. The proposal-types page dated 7 October nevertheless accepts General User and Rapid Access proposals for 34-ID-F. A December 2021 town hall addressed construction timing and scope. The December 2023 schedule proposed scientific commissioning in cycle 2025-1. December 2024 and January 2025 updates limited the initial completion scope to infrastructure. The August 2025 update expected first light in October and users late in run 2026-1. The October update reported the transition into commissioning. The 26 January 2026 chart still listed technical commissioning, stage 4. MEDSI 2025 reported that all nine feature beamlines met their Key Performance Parameters. Those criteria were brightness at a defined energy and usable energy range; only ISN had a focal-spot criterion. Meeting them therefore does not verify the 50 nm ATOMIC spot. The directory status remains 'Construction' and the feature page says 'Atomic (to come)', both behind the commissioning chart. No peer-reviewed post-upgrade ATOMIC result was found as of 9 October 2026. Highlights in 2026 credited to 34-ID-C appear to use pre-upgrade data. The project received final Department of Energy approval, CD-4, in January 2026, with full scope reported delivered.

tagline: Researchers reconstruct the three-dimensional shape and internal strain of individual nanocrystals from coherent X-ray diffraction measurements.
summary: At ATOMIC, researchers measure crystals smaller than a bacterium, including particles of battery material, catalyst and metal. Bragg coherent diffractive imaging, BCDI, uses a beam with a consistent phase relationship across it. At a crystal's Bragg angle, atomic planes diffract this light into intensity fringes. A detector records successive slices as the crystal rotates through a small angle. Software reconstructs crystal shape and atomic displacement from the measurements. Strain is calculated from displacement gradients and affects material performance and fracture. Bendable mirror pairs have a design spot range from 2 µm to 50 nm for crystals of different sizes. In October 2026, ATOMIC is in scientific commissioning.

whatAPSUEnables.text: Coherent imaging requires the fraction of X-rays with a consistent phase relationship across the beam. At the old APS, this was about 0.04% at 10 keV. In the design brightness mode, horizontal electron-beam width falls about nineteenfold, from 280 to 14.7 µm root-mean-square, and vertical width falls about threefold. The estimated coherent fraction rises to 5%. Slits select coherent illumination and mirrors focus it onto the crystal. At 8.7 keV, the design predicts 3.1 × 10¹² photons/s in a 0.1% band within a 50 nm spot. Operando three-dimensional resolution below 10 nm is targeted in tens of seconds. Increased heating, radiation damage and roughly four hundredfold data growth require attention. The quoted 540-fold coherent-flux gain at 20 keV assumes an undulator optimized there. Gain near ATOMIC's 9 keV operating energy is smaller. Measured post-upgrade performance is unpublished.
quantitative: Pre-upgrade operando scans at 34-ID-C took about two minutes per three-dimensional data set. The preliminary design targets resolution below 10 nm in tens of seconds.

Final-design Table 1.1 gives 3.12 × 10¹³ coherent photons/s at 20 keV in brightness mode, compared with 6 × 10¹⁰ before the upgrade. Their ratio is about 520; the report quotes 540. These values assume an undulator optimized for 20 keV rather than ATOMIC's 2.1 m revolver. Near 9 keV the gain is smaller. A derived 10 keV estimate combines a roughly 125-fold coherent-fraction gain with two- to threefold greater central-cone flux.
Horizontal electron-beam width changes from 280 to 14.7 µm root-mean-square, a nineteenfold reduction. Horizontal divergence changes from 11.6 to 2.8 µrad.

The derived coherent fraction at 10 keV for a 2.1 m undulator is about 5% in brightness mode, with horizontal fraction 0.11 and vertical fraction 0.48, compared with 0.04% before the upgrade. This uses final-design source parameters and photon contributions σr = √(2λL)/4π and σr' = √(λ/2L).

At 8.7 keV, final-design Table 4.65 predicts 3.1 × 10¹² photons/s in 50 nm and 4.6 × 10¹² in 2 µm, per 0.1% band, in brightness mode. Timing-mode predictions are 1.8 × 10¹² and 2.5 × 10¹² respectively.
Simulated spots at 8.7 keV range from 47 × 50 nm to 2.1 × 2.1 µm. The typical pre-upgrade spot was about 0.5 × 0.7 µm, horizontal by vertical. The smallest design spot has about 140 times less area.

The preliminary-design atomic-resolution estimate is about 1,000 s for a 50 nm volume with 4.9 × 10¹² photons/s focused into 50 nm. It uses Dietze and Shpyrko's dose estimate of about 10¹⁸ photons/µm² for a 20 nm gold crystal.
Expected annual data is 250 to 300 TB, compared with about 0.65 TB at 34-ID-C, a roughly four hundredfold increase.
The final-design resolution target is 1 nm or below. Typical third-generation BCDI has 10 to 30 nm three-dimensional resolution and about 2 × 10⁻⁴ strain resolution.

techniques.name: Bragg coherent diffractive imaging
techniques.text: Bragg coherent diffractive imaging, BCDI, uses an isolated crystal tens of nanometres to about 2 µm across. A coherent beam illuminates it at the angle for reflection from selected crystal planes. A small angular scan gives successive slices through a three-dimensional diffraction pattern. One 34-ID-C study used 76 one-second frames over ±0.3°. Only intensity is measured; iterative reconstruction recovers phase when each fringe spans at least two pixels in every direction. The reconstructed image gives shape and displacement perpendicular to the selected planes, to a fraction of an ångström, whose length is 0.1 nm. Displacement gradients give fractional strain near 10⁻⁴. Typical pre-upgrade spatial resolution was 10 to 30 nm. The ATOMIC target is 1 nm or below.

techniques.name: Laue-assisted multi-reflection coherent imaging
techniques.text: One Bragg reflection measures displacement along one direction. At least three reflections with non-coplanar directions are needed for all six components of stretch and shear. Pink beam first illuminates the crystal at many energies for a Laue pattern. LaueGo indexes the spots by atomic planes and determines orientation. The monochromator is then inserted for coherent imaging at three or more reflections. Heating its second crystal changes the exit angle to align the narrow-band and pink paths through the mirrors.

techniques.name: Bragg ptychography
techniques.text: For crystals or films larger than about 1.5 to 2 µm, diffraction is recorded at overlapping scan positions. The overlap supplies constraints for reconstruction of both the sample and illumination. Strain is then imaged over an area larger than one spot. Adjusting the mirror curvature changes the spot size and required number of scan positions. This is a planned mode with no documented commissioning at 34-ID-F.

techniques.name: Atomic-resolution wide-angle coherent imaging
techniques.text: The long-term target is three-dimensional atomic structure in crystalline and non-crystalline samples. Atomic-scale detail requires weak scattering far from the main reflection, near a scattering-vector magnitude of 1 Å⁻¹. This inverse-length quantity corresponds to atomic spacings. Intensity falls approximately as the inverse fourth power of distance from the reflection. Dietze and Shpyrko estimated about 10¹⁸ photons/µm² for a gold crystal and ten times less for an amorphous particle. The preliminary-design metallic-glass example requires roughly an hour for ten tomographic views. Atomic-resolution imaging is a future goal without an ATOMIC demonstration.

techniques.name: Polychromatic / pink-beam coherent imaging
techniques.text: Pink beam contains a wider energy band and more photons than monochromatic beam, increasing flux for weak or rapidly changing samples. The final design specifies a Pink Beam CDI mode. Mirror focusing is independent of energy, so the zoom optics accept an undulator harmonic's width. The preliminary design proposed reconstruction with multiple energies or coherent modes and broadband three-dimensional imaging without sample rotation. Operating status at 34-ID-F is unknown.

techniques.name: Operando coherent imaging and accelerated reconstruction
techniques.text: Samples are measured during operation in coin-cell batteries, gas-flow heaters up to 900 °C, cryogenic chambers near 80 K or liquid-flow cells. Equipment must fit within about 50 mm between the last mirror and focus. The cohere package performs iterative phase retrieval on graphics processors. Trained AutoPhaseNN reconstruction is reported about a hundred times faster than iterative methods; the 2024 computing strategy quotes more than ten times. Its output also supplies an initial estimate for iterative refinement. The physics-aware 3D-CDI-NN predicts structure and strain hundreds of times faster for feedback during measurement. Element-specific and polarization-sensitive imaging with a diamond phase plate appeared in the 2017 proposal. The final design omitted the plate.

scienceCases.title: Battery-particle strain and defects during cycling
scienceCases.text: Battery crystallites expand and contract during cycling. Internal defects affect degradation. Ulvestad and colleagues imaged dislocations appearing, moving and disappearing in lithium-nickel-manganese oxide nanoparticles inside a working cell at the APS in 2015. Later work, much at 34-ID-C, measured metastable dislocation loops in sodium-ion cathodes, solid-electrolyte defects and a phase boundary moving through a cathode particle. The latter required about two minutes per three-dimensional scan. The ATOMIC design targets operando resolution below 10 nm in tens of seconds with increased coherent flux and the 50 nm mirror focus.

scienceCases.title: Catalyst strain during chemical reactions
scienceCases.text: Catalytic reactions often concentrate at particle corners and edges. In 2016, Ulvestad and colleagues measured strain at gold-crystal corners during ascorbic-acid decomposition in particles about 300 nm across. Reactive molecular-dynamics calculations related it to surface-bound hydroxyl groups. A preliminary-design proposal would image electrochemical removal of silver from a silver-gold nanocrystal. Energy near the gold L₃ edge, about 12 keV, changes gold scattering for element-specific contrast. Subsequent measurements would follow catalysis and coarsening in the remaining nanoporous gold. Variable focus accommodates different particle sizes.

scienceCases.title: Defects in metals for fusion and aerospace
scienceCases.text: Defects influence metal response to heat and radiation. Hofmann and colleagues used Laue microdiffraction at 34-ID-E to locate tungsten dislocations in 2020. Focused-ion-beam cutting isolated microcrystals around them. Multi-reflection coherent imaging at 34-ID-C then determined the full stretch and shear tensor. Related studies at 10 to 30 nm resolution measured annealing of ion-beam damage in gold and corrosion in cobalt-iron. Yau and colleagues observed a dislocation loop entering a gold-film grain boundary near 400 °C at the APS in 2017. The ATOMIC design combines in situ Laue orientation with focus adjustment for grains within films.

scienceCases.title: Growth mechanisms recorded in crystal strain
scienceCases.text: Crystal strain and defects depend on mineral growth conditions. Yuan and colleagues measured calcite and barite growth, with and without strontium, using coherent imaging at 34-ID-C. Calcite retained many defects and lattice strain, consistent with growth from prenucleation clusters or disordered precursors. Barite grew classically by ion addition. Electron microscopy and molecular-dynamics calculations supported these interpretations. The work appeared in JACS in 2026.

scienceCases.title: Proposed atomic imaging of metallic-glass failure
scienceCases.text: Metallic glasses lack long-range crystalline order and may fail abruptly. A 2017 feasibility study modelled atomic imaging before a small pillar yields. Its 20 nm Cu₆₄Zr₃₆ pillar contained 96,000 atoms. Scattering out to 1.26 Å⁻¹ was calculated to locate atoms to 0.1 Å. With about 2 × 10¹² photons/s in a 0.01% band focused into 20 × 26 nm, each data set would take roughly seven minutes. About ten orientations per strain state would require an hour. Dietze and Shpyrko estimate ten times lower atomic-resolution dose for amorphous material than for crystals. This remains a proposed measurement.

scienceCases.title: Proposed imaging of spin-lattice coupling
scienceCases.text: In some oxides, magnetic order is coupled to lattice distortion. The 2017 proposal included resonant coherent imaging at an absorption edge to map antiferromagnetic twin domains in Sr₂IrO₄ as temperature and field change. Neighbouring magnetic moments in this material point in opposite directions. A diamond phase plate would supply circular polarization up to about 12 keV for comparisons between opposite polarizations. Proposed measurements would relate defects to magnetic structure. The final design omitted the phase plate, so this is a future option.

scienceCases.title: Reconstruction during measurements
scienceCases.text: Annual ATOMIC data is projected at 250 to 300 TB, about four hundred times 34-ID-C's 0.65 TB. Fast coherent imaging produces about 20 MB/s. The cohere package distributes phase retrieval across graphics processors. AutoPhaseNN and physics-aware 3D-CDI-NN, with automatic-differentiation refinement, reconstruct images rapidly enough for measurement decisions during an experiment. AutoFocus was developed using a simulation of the bendable mirrors at 34-ID-C and validated on a similar system at 28-ID-B.

insertionDevices.name: ATOMIC 21 mm revolver structure, APS21R25#8S and APS21#13S
insertionDevices.type: Planar hybrid permanent-magnet revolver with two structures on a rotating support and a shared four-motor gap mechanism
insertionDevices.polarization: Horizontal linear polarization from a planar device with vertical magnetic field
insertionDevices.notes: The downstream 34-ID device supplies inboard ATOMIC. The installed 21 mm structure has 98 periods, K = 1.38 and first harmonic 8.33 keV at the 8.5 mm device minimum gap. As K approaches zero, the first harmonic approaches 16 keV. At 200 mA, power is 4.8 kW and peak density 190 kW/mrad². The third harmonic covers about 25 keV and higher for the 30 keV upper range. Final-design mask-transmitted powers are 763 and 738 W for the two arrays at 30 m; their assignment is ambiguous in Table 4.62. The insertion-device table identifies a short device. The directory's 2.3 m length may include the overall mechanism. Administrative minimum gap is 8.65 mm, user minimum 9.0 mm. The tabulated K and first harmonic are at 8.5 mm. Hybrid-field scaling at the user gap gives estimated first harmonics of 8.9 to 9.1 keV for U21 and 5.0 to 5.1 keV for U25, consistent with the 5.3 keV lower operating range.

insertionDevices.name: ATOMIC 25 mm revolver structure, APS25#10S
insertionDevices.type: Alternative planar hybrid permanent-magnet structure in the same revolver
insertionDevices.notes: Only one structure is active at a time; rotation requires an open gap. The 25 mm structure has 82 periods, K = 1.99 and first harmonic 4.59 keV at minimum gap. Power is 7.0 kW with peak density 196 kW/mrad². It covers the low end of the 5.3 to 30 keV range. The revolver mechanism is described in final-design section 3-3.3.2.

insertionDevices.name: Partner 3DMN device, U28 planar undulator APS28#13S
insertionDevices.notes: The upstream source supplies outboard 3DMN. It has 74 periods, K = 2.48 and first harmonic 3.00 keV. It is included to explain the shared straight section.

source.canting: The source axes are separated by 1.0 mrad. Electromagnetic magnets deflect 0.5 mrad upstream, 1.0 mrad centrally and 0.5 mrad downstream, with a central corrector. These are specified in final-design Table 3.20 and the insertion-device configuration table. ATOMIC uses the downstream inboard source; 3DMN the upstream outboard source. Exit-mask openings at 25.4 m are about 25 mm apart, calculated from the angle. Before the upgrade, 34-ID-C coherent imaging used the upstream outboard beam and 34-ID-E the inboard beam.
source.frontEnd: The Canted Undulator Front End has limits of two 10 kW beams and 280 kW/mrad² peak density, with a windowless differential-pump exit. Components include clearing magnet, low-power photon shutter, storage-ring valve, burn-through mask, fixed masks, GRID fluorescence monitor XBPM1, exit-mask monitor XBPM2, photon shutter and safety shutters SS1 and SS2. The upstream mask at 19.4 m is rated for 418 W/mm² in a final-design superconducting-undulator case. This is not an ATOMIC operating value. The exit table in 34-ID-A has two 2 × 2 mm openings at 25.4 m and two 5 × 5 mm tungsten collimator openings at 26.1 m.
source.sourceSizeAndDivergence: Final-design Table 1.1 gives root-mean-square electron source values. Brightness mode with 324 bunches and 42 pm emittance has horizontal and vertical widths 14.7 and 3.2 µm, with divergences 2.8 and 1.3 µrad. Timing mode with 48 bunches and 32 pm gives 12.9 and 8.8 µm, with 2.5 and 3.7 µrad. Pre-upgrade widths are 280 and 10.0 µm, with 11.6 and 3.4 µrad. Derived Gaussian photon-source values for the 2.1 m revolver at 8.7 keV in brightness mode are about 14.8 and 3.8 µm, with 6.5 and 6.0 µrad divergence. Coherent fractions are about 12% horizontally and 51% vertically, or 6% total. Canted source points are roughly 1 m from the straight centre, where beta functions differ slightly.

branches.name: ATOMIC inboard canted branch, 34-ID-F
branches.description: White-beam slit S1 and mirror are in A. Shielded transport and masks pass through B. Position monitoring, S2, monochromator, first mirror pair and shutter occupy C. Shielded pipe crosses 3DMN enclosure E. The final pair, sample and detector diffractometers occupy new ATOMIC enclosure F.

branches.name: Partner 3DMN outboard canted branch, 34-ID-E
branches.description: Upstream U28 supplies 3DMN through the shared front end and A optics. Its outboard mirror is at 29.6 m, masks in B and monochromator in C at 53.8 m. The micro instrument is near 60 m in E, with a designed nano station near 65.5 m and installation unconfirmed. 3DMN has a separate exhibit.

components.name: Partner upstream U28 planar undulator for 3DMN
components.distanceNote: Upstream device of the same straight, centre ~-1.2 m from the straight centre, approx. as in the 3DMN exhibit.
components.text: The upstream undulator supplies 3DMN for multi-energy diffraction maps. Its 2.1 m magnetic structure has a 28 mm period. At an 8.5 mm gap, the first harmonic is near 3.0 keV. The source axes are separated by 1 mrad, with 3DMN outboard. It is included here to explain the shared source.

components.name: Canting magnets, 1 mrad
components.distanceNote: The central magnet defines distance zero. The two 0.5 mrad end magnets are approximately 2.45 m either side. Positions are not tabulated in final-design section 4-9.
components.text: Three electromagnets bend the electron orbit by 0.5, 1.0 and 0.5 mrad. The undulator axes are separated by 1 mrad, about 0.06°, giving about 25 mm beam separation at the front-end exit. Downstream ATOMIC is inboard; upstream 3DMN is outboard.

components.name: Revolver undulator U21/U25, downstream device, inboard beam
components.distanceNote: Exhibit distances refer to the centre of the 34-ID straight, as in the preliminary-design source definition and final-design Table 4.63. The downstream revolver centre is placed approximately 1.2 m from that origin. This may explain roughly 1 m differences between the ray-trace and plan frames.
components.text: This approximately 2.1 m revolver contains 21 and 25 mm-period permanent-magnet structures. Alternating fields bend stored electrons, and radiation from successive bends combines into a narrow beam. The support rotates 90° with the gap open to select the structure. Closing the gap lowers the first harmonic. At the 8.5 mm minimum gap, it is 8.33 keV for the 21 mm structure and 4.59 keV for the 25 mm structure. Higher odd harmonics extend across 5.3 to 30 keV. User gaps are at least 9.0 mm, giving slightly higher first-harmonic energies.

specs.swap: strongbacks rotate 90° with the gap open

components.name: Canted undulator front end, CUFE
components.distanceNote: The upstream front-end mask is documented at 19.4 m in the Chapter 3 beam-position-monitor power table. The front end extends through the tunnel to the wall near 24.4 m, with its exit table inside A. The schematic model spans 15.6 to 24.0 m and follows the design component order, from clearing magnet and low-power shutter through valves, masks, monitor, photon and safety shutters to differential pumps. Only the 19.4 m mask position is documented. Its 418 W/mm² rating is a superconducting-undulator design case rather than an ATOMIC operating value.
components.text: The front end connects the accelerator and beamlines inside the shielding tunnel. Masks absorb unwanted power; monitors measure position; photon and safety shutters block beam for access. The limit is 10 kW per beam. Differential pumping separates the vacuums without an exit window, avoiding disturbance of the coherent wavefront.

specs.XBPM: GRID XBPM1 + XBPM2 in exit mask
specs.elements: clearing magnet, low-power photon shutter, storage-ring valve, burn-through fixed mask, fixed masks, GRID XBPM1, photon and safety shutters

components.name: Front-end exit mask with XBPM2
components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.63.
components.text: The metal exit mask has two 2 mm square openings about 25 mm apart. The central part of each beam passes; the rest is absorbed. Monitor XBPM2 is integrated into the mask.

components.name: Front-end exit collimator
components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.63.
components.text: The tungsten exit collimator has a 5 mm square opening for each beam. It confines bremsstrahlung, high-energy radiation from stored-electron interactions with residual gas. The reduced upgrade openings accommodate the approximately 1 mm monochromator offsets.

components.name: White-beam slits S1, inboard, 34ID-SL-1
components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.63, PDR: ~27 m.
components.text: Tungsten-edged slits S1 limit ATOMIC white beam at 26.8 m. A small opening forms a secondary source for coherent illumination downstream. A larger opening gives greater flux with partial coherence. The second aperture, S2, is 23.5 m downstream.

specs.mode: closed: secondary source; open: partially coherent beam

components.name: Tungsten bremsstrahlung collimator, 34ID-BC-1
components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.63.
components.text: The tungsten shield at 28.4 m confines bremsstrahlung around both beam paths. A lead collimator follows for additional shielding.

components.name: Lead bremsstrahlung collimator, 34ID-BC-2
components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.63.
components.text: The lead shield at 28.7 m has openings for both beams. Together with the tungsten block, it confines accelerator radiation before the mirrors.

components.name: Partner 3DMN outboard white-beam mirror, 34ID-MR-1
components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.63.
components.text: The neighbouring 3DMN mirror reflects outboard at 3.0 mrad grazing incidence. ATOMIC passes about 30 mm inboard of it. After both branch mirrors, the beams diverge by about 13 mrad. This mirror is included for shared-layout context.

components.name: Inboard white-beam mirror, 34ID-MR-2
components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.63, PDR: 31 m. The 3DMN outboard mirror sits at 29.6 m.
components.text: The flat silicon mirror reflects ATOMIC inboard at 3.0 mrad grazing incidence, about 0.17°. Reflectivity falls above a coating-dependent critical energy, rejecting higher harmonics. Vertical translation selects silicon, rhodium or platinum stripes with estimated cutoffs near 10, 22 and 28 keV. A substrate notch reduces absorbed-heat deformation.

components.name: Secondary bremsstrahlung collimator, 34ID-SC-2
components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.63, branch not stated; follows the ATOMIC mirror, by analogy with SC-1 after the 3DMN mirror.
components.text: This collimator confines bremsstrahlung after the mirror. X-rays reflect by 6 mrad while the high-energy radiation continues straight into the shielding.

components.name: Diagnostic flag, 34ID-BD-1
components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.63.
components.text: A fluorescent screen moves into the beam for alignment. A camera records the visible emission at the X-ray position. The flag is after both white-beam mirrors and retracts during experiments.

components.name: Pink photon mask / white-beam stop, 34ID-PM-1
components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.63.
components.text: The stop absorbs straight-through white beam, the full undulator spectrum. Openings transmit reflected pink beam after the mirrors have rejected the highest energies.

components.name: Shielded transport 34-ID-A to 34-ID-B, 34ID-ST-1
components.distanceNote: Spans 36.0 to 42.5 m, FDR Table 4.63; existing white-beam shielded transport reused.
components.text: The reused 6.5 m lead-shielded pipe transports both reflected beams across open floor from 34-ID-A to 34-ID-B. Its shielding permits use of the surrounding floor during operation.

components.name: Laue orientation detector, Eiger 500K
components.distanceNote: At the predecessor station, the Laue detector was about 25 mm from the focus on the inboard side facing outboard, with vertical and lateral motion. Pateras and colleagues' 2020 Timepix arrangement was 26 mm from rotation centre, above and inboard. The ATOMIC position is unpublished. The illustrative model follows the predecessor, with the sensor about 28 mm from the sample and centre 30 mm downstream at beam height. This accepts forward Laue scattering and clears the final mirrors.
components.text: The nearby Eiger 500K records Laue patterns for orientation. Multi-energy illumination diffracts from many sets of atomic planes simultaneously. Indexing these spots determines the angles for subsequent coherent reflections. The detector has 1024 × 512 pixels of 75 µm. At 34-ID-C it was about 25 mm from the sample.

components.distanceNote: Near the sample, approx.. Drawn on the outboard side at 90° to the beam in the horizontal plane, where elastic scattering of the horizontally polarized beam is weakest, illustrative position.

The model position is sideways at 90° in the horizontal plane, where elastic scattering of horizontally polarized light is weakest. The predecessor instrument used a Vortex EX-60 silicon drift detector.

components.name: Detector-positioning diffractometer, detector arm
components.distanceNote: The arm pivots at the 69.5 m sample. Preliminary-design length is 4500 mm. The final-design plan shows about 35° outboard with a floor radius near 4.1 to 4.3 m across roughly 8 to 67°. The illustrative model has a 4.4 m boom at horizontal δ = 30° outboard and vertical γ = 16.8°, giving 2θ = 34.0° for Au 111 at 9 keV. As-built geometry is unpublished.
components.text: The detector arm positions an area detector at selected scattering angles and distances up to about 5 m. Larger crystals produce more closely spaced fringes, requiring greater distance for several pixels per fringe. Five metres accommodates crystals up to about 1.5 to 2 µm in a single-view coherent measurement. Horizontal polarization favours high-angle scattering vertically. The predecessor arm reached 150° vertically and 45° horizontally. The new arm's operating geometry is unpublished.

components.distanceNote: The predecessor used a tube along the diffracted path. The illustrative model spans 0.35 to 2.85 m from the sample at 2θ = 34°. Its midpoint has along-beam coordinate 70.8 m. Presence and length on the new arm are unpublished.
components.text: Vacuum between sample and detector reduces air absorption and scattering background, improving measurements of weak outer fringes. A flight tube was used at 34-ID-C for roughly 1 m sample-to-detector distance. Its presence and length at ATOMIC are unpublished.

instruments.name: ATOMIC coherent-imaging endstation, final design
instruments.text: In 34-ID-F, separate sample and detector diffractometers position a crystal and detector for coherent imaging. The design focus ranges from 50 nm to 2 µm; detector distance reaches about 5 m. The final design includes a beam-conditioning platform and independent Monochromatic CDI and Pink Beam CDI modes. The 2017 concept specifies in situ Laue orientation and sample stability of tens of nanometres over an hour. As-built hardware remains unpublished as of October 2026. The directory lists access to a scanning electron microscope for sample characterization.

instruments.name: Pre-upgrade 34-ID-C coherent-imaging instrument
instruments.text: The first three-dimensional strain image within a nanocrystal was demonstrated here in 2006. Operation continued until the 2023 upgrade shutdown. The former hutch now contains ATOMIC's monochromator and first mirror pair. Pre-upgrade bendable mirrors focused to about 0.5 × 0.7 µm. Monochromator retraction provided pink beam for Laue orientation. Detector distances were 0.5 to 2.5 m. The 5 mrad platinum mirror limited practical energy to about 17 keV. Software, methods and probably hardware transferred to ATOMIC. The 34-ID-F directory's five-circle instrument, 70 mm working distance and roughly 300 nm spot appear to describe the predecessor setup.
detectors: Vortex EX-60 silicon drift detector, SDD

geometryNotes:
The downstream 34-ID revolver supplies the inboard ATOMIC beam. The upstream 28 mm-period device supplies outboard 3DMN, separated by 1.0 mrad. Before the upgrade, coherent-imaging station 34-ID-C used the outboard beam with a further 10 mrad outboard reflection, as documented in the 2013 beamline wiki.

The existing experiment-floor footprint contains 34-ID-A from about 24.4 to 36.0 m, shielded transport from 36.0 to 42.5 m, B from 42.3 to 47.8 m, C from 47.8 to 55.0 m, E from 55.0 to 67.5 m, and new F from 67.5 to about 79.8 m. C is the shared optics station in the former coherent-imaging room. E houses 3DMN and ATOMIC transport about 0.4 m inboard. Boundaries are remeasured from final-design Fig. 4.58 at about 25 pixels/m and matched to the 3DMN dossier. The C/E wall lies between shutters at 54.8 m and transport start at 55.1 m.

In the 2017 preliminary design, the second optics enclosure was B, 3DMN was D and ATOMIC was E. In the 2019 final design, these assignments are C, E and F.

The ATOMIC flat mirror at 31.3 m reflects inboard at 3.0 mrad grazing incidence, for 6 mrad deflection. The opposing 3DMN reflection is outboard. These directions appear in final-design Fig. 4.59 and preliminary-design text. Including source canting, derived separation is about 11 mrad at the preliminary 2.5 mrad incidence, or 13 mrad at 3.0 mrad. The plan depicts about 0.4 m separation in E. The horizontal monochromator shifts narrow-band beam sideways about 1.1 mm.

Each focusing pair deflects in both planes by about 6 mrad at 3 mrad incidence, or up to 10 mrad at 5 mrad incidence. The final axis is therefore tilted slightly in an unpublished direction. Beam height is approximately the APS standard 1.4 m, consistent with the preliminary-design elevation.

In F, the plan-scaled beam path is about 2 m from the straight inboard wall. The enclosure is about 7.5 m wide upstream, narrowing along a diagonal outboard wall, with a step near 74.8 m, to about 2 m near 79.8 m. The diffractometer is near 69.5 to 69.7 m. Its arm is labelled 4500 mm in the preliminary design; final-design plan radius is about 4.2 to 4.4 m. The plan shows an outboard sweep. The elevation gives about 3.5 m roof height here versus 2.6 m upstream for vertical detector motion. The pink-beam stop is at 78.7 m.

The first mirror pair is at 52.0 m in a table, 54 m in drawings and text, or 52.7 to 53.2 m in the ray-trace frame. The second is tabulated at 68.1 m, whereas its 0.12 and 0.4 m image distances imply about 69.1 to 69.4 m for a 69.5 m sample. The ray-trace origin appears roughly 1.1 m nearer the downstream undulator. The exhibit follows the drawing frame, with the first pair near 54 m and the second immediately before the 69.5 m sample, at about 50 mm working distance.

Incident polarization is horizontal. Grazing mirrors are effectively insensitive to polarization. The horizontal Si(111) monochromator reflects π polarization, with bandwidth and throughput proportional to |cos 2θB|, calculated near 0.72 at 5.3 keV and 0.92 at 10 keV.

For horizontal sample scattering, the kinematic factor is cos²(2θ), about 0.69 for Au 111 at 9 keV and 0.25 to 0.02 across 2θ = 60 to 80°. The pre-upgrade arm therefore reached high angles mainly vertically, with γ up to 150° compared with horizontal δ up to 45°.

interactiveIdeas.title: Crystal shape, displacement and diffraction
interactiveIdeas.concept: Visitors deform a model nanocrystal by compressing a corner, adding a dislocation or adsorbing molecules on a face. The corresponding two- and three-dimensional Bragg intensity changes. A 'reconstruct' button runs several hundred error-reduction and hybrid-input-output iterations. Reconstructed phase is coloured as displacement along the reflection vector G.
interactiveIdeas.whatUserLearns: The reconstructed amplitude gives crystal shape. Phase gives displacement along the selected reflection direction. Changes in the diffraction pattern depend on both shape and displacement.
interactiveIdeas.physicsToGetRight: Near reflection G, I(q) = |FT{ρ(r) exp(i G·u(r))}|² and phase φ = G·u. For Au(111), d = 2.355 Å, so one radian corresponds to d/(2π) = 0.375 Å displacement, with phase wrapping every 2.355 Å. Strain ε_zz = (1/|G|)dφ/dz. Bragg's law gives 2θ = 34.0° for Au(111) at 9 keV. Oversampling must be at least two in each dimension. Fringe spacing is λD/s; a 300 nm crystal at 9 keV and 1.1 m gives about 505 µm, roughly nine 55 µm pixels. Reconstruction ambiguities include overall phase, conjugate inversion and translation. A rocking scan about 0.3 to 1° samples the third direction. Typical current resolution is 10 to 30 nm. Atomic structure should appear only in a clearly identified future mode.

interactiveIdeas.title: Two-stage mirror focusing
interactiveIdeas.concept: A side view shows the roughly 15 m separation of the mirror pairs. Changing first-pair curvature moves the intermediate focus between them. The display calculates illumination of the final pair, numerical aperture, focal width from 50 nm to 2 µm, and flux. A sample-size control compares illumination and crystal dimensions.
interactiveIdeas.whatUserLearns: Changing mirror curvature changes spot width while the sample focus remains fixed. A small diffraction-limited spot requires broad illumination of the final mirrors. Matching spot and crystal dimensions reduces light outside the sample.
interactiveIdeas.physicsToGetRight: Final-design Fig. 4.64 gives first-mirror length 350 mm at source distance about 53 m and about 15 m between pairs. Final horizontal length is 140 mm with image distance 0.12 m and about 50 mm working distance. Vertical length is 400 mm with image distance 0.4 m. Incidence is 3 mrad. Projected acceptance is Lθ, about 1 mm for the first mirrors. For a uniformly illuminated one-dimensional aperture, full width at half maximum is about 0.44 λ/NA, with NA = L_illuminated θ/(2q). At 8.7 keV, a 50 nm spot requires about 1.25 mrad. Full final-mirror apertures give 1.75 mrad horizontally and 1.5 mrad vertically. Preliminary outgoing divergence is about 2.3 × 2.5 mrad for 50 nm and 65 × 70 µrad for 1.5 µm. Source-image magnification M = (q1/p1)(q2/p2) is below the diffraction width at the small setting. Use diffraction to model that limit. Figure error must be below 1 nm root-mean-square. Design flux at 8.7 keV is 3.1 × 10¹² photons/s for 50 nm and 4.6 × 10¹² for 2 µm, per 0.1% band.

interactiveIdeas.title: Coherent fraction before and after the upgrade
interactiveIdeas.concept: Visitors compare old electron widths of 280 × 10 µm with upgraded widths of 14.7 × 3.2 µm, both root-mean-square. After 50 m propagation, a double slit or nanocrystal gives interference. S1 and S2 controls compare transmitted flux and fringe visibility.
interactiveIdeas.whatUserLearns: Coherent illumination produces high-contrast fringes. The estimated coherent-fraction increase near 10 keV is roughly a hundredfold, giving greater usable flux after coherence selection.
interactiveIdeas.physicsToGetRight: Photon widths are Σ = √(σe² + σr²) and Σ' = √(σe'² + σr'²), with σr = √(2λL)/4π, σr' = √(λ/(2L)) and L = 2.1 m. Coherent fraction per plane is (λ/4π)/(ΣΣ'). At 10 keV, derived brightness-mode fractions are about 0.11 horizontally and 0.48 vertically, compared with about 0.003 and 0.16 before the upgrade. One transverse-coherence convention gives length λz/(2πΣ), about 70 µm horizontally at 50 m and 10 keV, compared with 3.5 µm before. Longitudinal coherence λ²/(2Δλ) is about 0.5 µm for Si(111) at 10 keV. Sample path differences must be smaller. Table 1.1 gives about 520-fold coherent-flux gain at 20 keV for its optimized undulator.

interactiveIdeas.title: Dose and resolution
interactiveIdeas.concept: Visitors adjust desired resolution from 30 nm to 0.2 nm. The display calculates required scattering range, weak outer intensity, dose and collection time before and after the upgrade. Sample heating and radiation damage are shown as physical limits.
interactiveIdeas.whatUserLearns: Fine spatial detail requires sufficient counts at high scattering angles. Detector rate and sample survival constrain dose, especially for proposed atomic-resolution measurements.
interactiveIdeas.physicsToGetRight: Half-period resolution is about π/q_max; the minimum sampled lattice period is 2π/q_max. For q_max = 1.26 Å⁻¹, half-period resolution is about 2.5 Å. The compact-object envelope falls roughly as q⁻⁴ under Porod scaling. At fixed signal per volume element, required dose scales approximately as resolution⁻⁴. Dietze and Shpyrko estimate about 10¹⁸ photons/µm² for a 20 nm gold crystal and 10¹⁷ for amorphous gold. At 3.1 × 10¹² photons/s in 50 × 50 nm, flux density is about 1.2 × 10¹⁵ photons/s/µm². The larger dose takes about 800 s, compared with the preliminary 1,000 s estimate. Preliminary focused power at 10 keV is about 8 mW. Heating and damage must be included. The worst-case unattenuated transmitted beam at 0.2 m gives about 7 × 10¹⁰ photons/s per 75 µm pixel, compared with a 3 × 10⁶ linear limit. Bragg-reflection fringes are much weaker.

interactiveIdeas.title: Laue orientation before coherent imaging
interactiveIdeas.concept: Visitors first record and index a pink-beam Laue pattern from a submicrometre grain on a substrate. They then position the distant detector and rotate the sample for a selected coherent reflection. Three non-coplanar reflections are selected for reconstruction of the full strain tensor.
interactiveIdeas.whatUserLearns: Laue indexing gives orientation before narrow-band coherent imaging. A nearby detector accepts many Laue reflections. Three non-coplanar reflection directions are needed for the complete displacement and strain field.
interactiveIdeas.physicsToGetRight: The predecessor pink spectrum was roughly 5 to 20 keV. Reciprocal-lattice points between the limiting Ewald spheres diffract simultaneously. With known energy calibration, orientation accuracy near 0.01° is possible. Heating the second monochromator crystal aligns pink and narrow-band illumination. Each reflection measures u·G_hkl. Three non-coplanar vectors determine u(r) and the six-component strain tensor. The preliminary design gives Au 333 and 400 angles near 60 to 80° at 12 keV. For horizontal polarization, horizontal scattering has the cos²(2θ) intensity factor. Vertical detector travel is preferable at high angles; the predecessor vertical range reached 150°.

funFacts: The first 3D image of the strain field inside a single nanocrystal, a lead crystal, was made at 34-ID-C, ATOMIC's predecessor, and published in Nature in 2006.
The name Atomic refers to the future goal of wavelength-limited atomic-resolution coherent imaging. The proposal began as upgrade white paper WP28 in January 2016.
The 2019 design repurposed the former 34-ID-C experiment hutch for the monochromator and first mirror pair. The new experiment station is downstream in 34-ID-F.
ATOMIC and 3DMN share a roughly 5 m straight section. Their axes differ by 1 mrad, giving about 2.5 cm separation after 25 m.
The revolver contains 21 and 25 mm-period magnet structures on a support that rotates 90° to select one.

Root-mean-square shape errors must stay below 1 nm during bending of mirrors up to 40 cm long. For comparison, the preliminary design quotes roughly 30 nm figure error for the Hubble Space Telescope mirror while discussing sample-stage stability.

The worst-case design calculation uses an unattenuated transmitted 50 nm beam on 75 µm pixels at 20 cm. It gives about 7 × 10¹⁰ photons/s per pixel, roughly 20,000 times the Eiger-class linear count limit.
Projected annual data is 250 to 300 TB, roughly four hundred times the predecessor's 0.65 TB.
The preliminary design estimates about 8 mW in a 50 × 50 nm spot at 10 keV. Sample heating therefore matters even at milliwatt power.
A 2017 Science study of a heated gold film reached 10 nm spatial resolution and sub-ångström displacement sensitivity with coherent imaging.

openQuestions: As-built sample and detector hardware is unpublished. Unknowns include diffractometer geometry and vendor, transfer of the predecessor five-circle instrument, arm length and angular ranges, and construction of the proposed inverted-joystick goniometer. High-angle vertical scattering is preferred for horizontal polarization. The new arm's vertical and horizontal motion is unconfirmed.

Both mirror pairs' installation, commissioning, bender or bimorph mechanism, and measured spot range are unconfirmed. The 2020 1-BM prototype reached micrometre spots limited by shape error. AutoFocus in 2023 used the predecessor mirror simulation.

The first pair is at 52.0 m in Table 4.63, 54 m in text and drawings, or 52.7 to 53.2 m in ray tracing. The second is tabulated at 68.1 m; image distances 0.12 and 0.4 m imply about 69.1 to 69.4 m for a 69.5 m sample. The ray-trace sample at 68.4 m and tabulated 69.5 m remain unreconciled.

The 2026 directory lists TimePix2 with 512 × 512 pixels of 55 µm and an Eiger 500K for Laue only. Detector purchases were removed from the upgrade scope in 2024. No Lambda installation was found. Use of Eiger2 4M, 500K or another high-rate coherent-imaging detector is unknown.

The 5 October 2026 chart lists stage 5 commissioning and early experiments, and proposals are accepted from 7 October. General-user restart at stage 6 and first post-upgrade publications are unconfirmed. Directory Construction and feature-page to come labels are behind the commissioning record.

The final design gives 2.1 m magnetic length, consistent with 98 × 21 mm and 82 × 25 mm period counts. The directory gives 2.3 m, possibly overall length. Table 4.62 does not clearly associate 763/738 W and K = 1.939/1.305 with individual structures.

The directory has an unspecified multilayer-monochromator entry. The preliminary design proposed this optional device and a diamond phase plate, neither listed in the final design. Installation of either is unknown.

The white-beam mirror is specified to reflect inboard in final-design Fig. 4.59 and preliminary-design section 6-3.4.1. Final-mirror deflection directions and sample beam height and offsets remain unpublished.
Widths, roof height and arm sweep are scaled from low-resolution drawings with about ±0.3 m uncertainty or worse. Preliminary and final outlines differ.

December 2024 and January 2025 updates limited project delivery to 3DMN and ATOMIC infrastructure, while MEDSI 2025 reports compliance with all feature-beamline performance criteria. The component split between project and operations funding is unclear.

The final design and directory give 5.3 to 30 keV, compared with the preliminary 5 to 25 keV. Actual upper energy depends on stripe and harmonic selection and is unpublished. A derived platinum cutoff near 28 keV at 3.0 mrad means five reflections at 30 keV require smaller angles or give low throughput.
Availability of pink-beam coherent imaging and Bragg ptychography to users in 2026 is unconfirmed.
